1.pericope_label: The Danites seek land, and their spies consult Micah's oracle

schools.summary: Gill reads the note that there was no king as an explanation offered in advance, the period lying after Joshua and before Othniel, so that the theft of Micah's priest and gods and the setting up of the image in Dan spread an idolatry which brought on the servitude Othniel was raised to end. Of the oracle he leaves the door open both ways, that the priest spoke either of his own head or by a voice which Satan might be permitted to deliver.

Henry supplies the motive for the tribe's long delay, that the city lay far off and wholly in enemy hands, so they preferred to sponge upon their brethren until necessity roused them — better, he adds, to have a little of one's own than always to hang upon others. He admires the choice of scouts, men of valour who if taken knew how to look danger in the face, since it is prudent to look before we leap, and finds in Dan the subtlety of a serpent as well as the courage of a lion's whelp. On the consultation he has no patience: they would never have enquired of God at all had the sight of the teraphim not put it into their heads, like the many who never think of religion except when it falls in their way; they supposed that God, having forbidden graven images, would answer them through one; they had passed Shiloh without enquiring of the high priest there, thinking better of Micah's teraphim than of God's urim; and the Levite, whether he believed it himself or not, humoured them so well that they took his word for God's.

Clarke observes that the Hebrew word for men of valour covers personal prowess, mental energy and earthly substance alike, and that they knew the Levite by his pronunciation to be no Ephraimite, that tribe having already been caught out by a syllable. On the oracle he argues the case for its genuineness against those who deny it: the Danites say Elohim and the priest answers before Jehovah, a name never given to any but the true God, and the venture succeeded exactly as the oracle said, so that it is begging the question to call the answer a trick of the Levite or a suggestion of the devil and the success accidental, which is to take the thing by the worst handle to prop up a system.

Ellicott is precise about the landlessness: the inheritance had been assigned, but they could not conquer it against the Philistines and the Amorites, and the English version interpolates the words all their before inheritance to smooth the difficulty — a well-meant gloss, but such glosses violate the translator's first duty, which is to be rigidly faithful. He finds the failure the more remarkable because in the wilderness Dan had been the strongest of the tribes and had received the smallest allotment. On the recognition of the Levite he thinks acquaintance more likely than accent, since Jonathan had lived at Bethlehem and Dan and Judah had close intercourse then, though he prefers the supposition that they heard him at his service before the image, and records Cassel's rendering of the word as sound rather than voice, referred to the bells of the priestly dress. Of the oracle he says they might at least have consulted Phinehas, and hears in the reply the ambiguity proper to an oracle, Jonathan staking nothing on any definite detail. Keil takes the phrase about their coasts to mean out of their whole body, and reads the young man's dialect as showing him no native of those mountains.

debates.question: Was the Levite’s oracle a true answer from God?

sides.position: yes, on the evidence of the divine name used and of the venture succeeding exactly as promised; to call it a trick or a diabolical suggestion is to beg the question

7.pericope_label: Laish surveyed, the report brought back, and the six hundred set out

schools.summary: Gill measures the stages of the march from Bunting, sixteen miles to Kirjath-jearim for the first day and eight more to mount Ephraim.

Henry says that never was a place so ill governed nor so ill guarded. The want of a magistrate he takes for the heart of it: rulers are heirs of restraint, entrusted with an entail of power for the checking of what is evil, and though only grace can renew a depraved mind, the magistrate's hand may tie it, so that the wickedness of the wicked is neither so injurious nor so infectious as it would else be; and he notes the method the verse names, that of putting men to shame, so that those not held back by the shamefulness of the sin may be held by the shamefulness of the punishment. Of their security he has the gates open and the walls out of repair, and reads it as a sign that Israel, through sloth and cowardice, was no longer the terror to Canaan it had been; their having no business with any man he takes either for idleness, since they followed no trade and so grew unable to defend themselves, or for the independency they affected, so that they cared for nobody and nobody cared for them. He credits the spies with honesty, since the tribe had formed notions of insuperable difficulty and the report was framed with that discouragement in view — these, he says, were not in this evil spies.

Clarke supposes Laish a colony from Sidon which imitated the mother city's ease without her defences, and draws the military conclusion, that it could be struck before the news of invasion reached Sidon. On the last clause he prefers the Greek, which reads that they had no dealings with Syria, Aram and Adam differing by a single letter often indiscernible in manuscript; Laish lay on the Syrian frontier, so its isolation from the one neighbour that could have relieved it becomes a further reason for the Danites' confidence. Of the spies' speech he says it was plain and nervous, and took effect at once; of the six hundred, that these were the armed men only.

Ellicott finds the clause about the magistrate almost unreadable and suspects the text corrupt, the versions differing widely; as it stands he takes it to mean that no one possessing wealth among them did harm in any matter, the Greek giving heir of treasure. He places the town as the Leshem of Joshua, now Tel el-Kadi, the mound of the judge, northernmost city of Palestine, at the head of the chief stream of the Jordan, its position on a round hill girt with trees bearing out the description entirely; he renders the large land as wide on both hands, which Keil explains as room both to settle and to spread; and he insists that the expedition was no raid but the migration of a section of the tribe with wives, children and goods, rendering the word for appointed as girded. Keil renders the spies' opening as a rebuke, that the brethren stand silent, and traces their confidence that God had given the place into their hands back to the Levite's oracle; he and Ellicott both reason from the permanence of the name Mahaneh-dan that the halt was no single night's bivouac but a stay of some length.

debates.question: What does the clause about no magistrate mean?

sides.position: that there was no ruler to restrain evil, the office being an entail of power for that purpose
the text is almost certainly corrupt; as it stands it seems to say that no one of wealth among them did harm in any matter

debates.question: Had Laish no business with any man, or none with Syria?

sides.position: the Greek reading with Syria is to be preferred, Aram and Adam differing by one easily confused letter, and the isolation from Syria explains the Danites’ confidence

14.pericope_label: The images stolen and the priest bought over

schools.summary: Gill reconstructs the manoeuvre by which the priest came to be outside his own sanctuary: the five went first to the house, saluted the young man, told him a body of their brethren at the gate would be glad to see him, and walked him down, then, having introduced him, slipped back. He reads the gladness of the priest's heart as of a piece with a covetous and unsettled temper.

Henry grants one point and denies the rest: it was right to want God's presence, but wretchedly wrong to take for tokens of it images fitter for a puppet-play than for devotion; they wanted an oracle for company and for a council of war, and reckoned that men settling so far from Shiloh had more need of a house of gods than Micah, who lived close by it — only the reputation the things had lately acquired amusing them into a veneration they would have dropped had they thought to ask where the images came from. Of the theft he says the priest's negligence lost them, since while he sauntered at the gate and gazed at the strangers his treasure was gone; and he turns the whole into an indictment, that these gods could not keep themselves from being stolen and the Danites were sottish to think such protectors could protect them, their idolatry beginning in theft, a fit prologue to such an opera, since to break the second commandment they began with the eighth. On the buying of the priest he sets out the terms as preferment: it is more honour and profit to be chaplain to a regiment — for a regiment was all they were, though they called themselves a tribe — than domestic chaplain to a private gentleman.

Clarke suspects the design of carrying off priest and furniture was formed already, names Harpocrates, the god of silence, shown with a finger pressed to his lips, as the parallel to the gesture that opened the negotiation, and has the priest step into the crowd so as not to be spotted by Micah's household.

Ellicott glosses the invitation to consider as meaning whether and how to possess themselves of the things, and finds in these Danite freebooters the mixture of superstition with lawlessness, of robbery with devotion, often remarked in Greek and Italian brigands. He suggests the ephod habitually hung upon the carved image, so that whoever carried off the one carried off the other; calls the gesture of silence one of the most universal, and the attitude of the Egyptian Horus; and judges the alacrity with which the priest sanctions the theft very unworthy of a grandson of Moses, setting beside it Dean Stanley's parallel of the bribe offered in 1176 to the monk Roger of Canterbury. Keil puts the spies' hint plainly — do not lose this chance of getting a worship of our own for the new settlement — observes that the five went up, so Micah's house of God must have occupied an upper room, and notices that the grammar answers the difficulty of the priest's absence, the narrative passing into perfects which set the coming and the taking inside the same stretch of time as his standing at the gate.

21.pericope_label: Micah pursues the Danites and is sent home

schools.summary: Gill allows an interval before Micah even knew that his gods were gone and his priest decoyed away, and a further interval to collect servants and neighbours. He points out that ownership was the best argument Micah had and a poor one for the divinity of the images, and thinks it astonishing that a man should call them gods when he knew their making and had seen they could not save themselves from theft; and he has the Danites decline further talk with a man they thought impertinent, bidding him do his worst.

Clarke gives first the sense of substance or precious things for the last item in the baggage train, which the Vulgate has as everything that was precious, but prefers the baggage, what Caesar calls impedimenta and the Greek renders weight, warning that no wheeled carriage is to be imagined. He will not allow the worst sense to Micah's word: being a worshipper of the true God, he cannot mean idols by his elohim, but the representations of divine things and symbols of the divine presence. Of the Danites' threat he says what it is — a man must bear the loss of his substance or lose his life besides, the plain language of a highwayman.

Ellicott observes that it is only in this incidental way that the narrative lets slip that a whole migration is on the road, and sets the two readings of the baggage side by side, the Alexandrine manuscript giving their glorious possession and the Vatican the weight, inclining to the latter since the root means to be heavy. He explains why the overtaking was easy, the Danite march being slowed by women, children and cattle, and remarks that Micah's establishment was probably strong enough against ordinary robbers but that nobody could have looked for a raid of six hundred. He hears grim humour in the exchange, with a note of irony at Micah's discomfiture, and finds Dan behaving exactly as the blessing had described him, a serpent on the way and an adder in the path; on the phrase my gods which I made he takes the opposite line to Clarke, that Micah does not scruple to call them his gods, as the idolater Laban had done, and that the phrase looks meant to hold him up to scorn, the Greek softening it to my graven image and the Chaldee to my fear — to a Greek, who called a sculptor a god-maker, it would be unremarkable, but on an Israelite's lips it is startling. He ends generously, hoping Micah's loss proved his gain. Keil notes that the children, cattle and valuables went in front because the Danites feared an attack from the rear, decides that the word means the valuables and not the heavy baggage, reads the two clauses of the pursuit as circumstantial, and renders the threat as an order to be silent on pain of life, closing the episode with Micah seeing they were stronger than he and turning home.

27.pericope_label: Laish smitten and rebuilt as Dan

schools.summary: Gill supposes Laish to have stood under Sidonian protection, so that the suddenness of the attack left no time to send for help, and reads the new name as showing that the settlers still belonged to a tribe lying far to the south-west of them.

Henry opens with the moral of an unpunished march: meeting no disaster on the road, the Danites perhaps concluded they had done no wrong in robbing Micah, since many justify themselves in their impiety by their prosperity. The state of Laish he reads as the opposite warning, the people being quiet and secure and so easy prey to a handful of men, for many are brought to destruction by their security and Satan gets his advantage when we are careless. That they met no resistance he explains from the ledger of two nations, the measure of Canaanite iniquity being full while the Danites' was only beginning to fill. Of the renaming he says they called it Dan as a witness that, separated as they now were by the length of the land, they were Danites by birth, and draws the application that we should not lose the privilege of our relation to God's Israel but take every occasion to own it. He closes on the irony of the settlement, that God kept his promise and put them in possession, which bound them to be faithful, and the first thing they did was to break his statutes, attributing to an image a success which, had God been less patient, that image would have cost them.

Clarke says the spies' report proved correct, the people apprehending no danger and unprepared to resist, and that the Sidonians were simply too far off to be of use; he observes what the name Dan afterwards became, one of the two ends of the land, the extent of the whole being commonly given as from Dan to Beersheba.

Ellicott stops at the burning, which he calls unusual, Hazor being the one city Joshua is recorded to have burnt, and offers three possibilities — a ban like Jericho's, a purpose of policy, or accident — adding that the thought of such conduct being cruel probably never crossed their minds, so we must not judge them by the standard of Christian times. He does not leave the tribe unjudged: Dan was no gainer, the name dropping out of the genealogies in Chronicles and missing from the sealed tribes in the Revelation, and he cites Blunt's conjecture that the disappearance came of intermarriage with the Phoenicians. He puts the site at the foot of the lowest range of Lebanon, notes that Beth-rehob means house of spaciousness, and records Robinson's identification of it with Hunin, a fortress commanding the plain; the renaming he compares to the Messenians, who changed Zankle into Messene. Keil sets the town in the valley stretching to Beth-rehob, the upper part of the Huleh lowland through which the central source of the Jordan runs, and identifies Beth-rehob with the Rehob of the spies' report in Numbers.

debates.question: Why was the city burnt, when burning was not the usual practice?

sides.position: either they had devoted it by a ban as Jericho was devoted, or the fire served a purpose of policy, or it was accidental

30.pericope_label: The image set up at Dan, and the priesthood of Jonathan

schools.summary: Gill supposes a house was built for the image in the new city, probably where Jeroboam afterwards set up one of his calves; the Danites, having prospered exactly as the oracle promised, held the things they had carried off in great veneration, and though only the graven image is named he takes it that the molten image, the teraphim and the ephod stood with it.

Clarke says they erected a chapel of their own as Micah had, with the same furniture and the same priest, and observes that no Manasseh will fit the genealogy — not the son of Joseph, who had no son called Gershom, nor the king, who lived eight centuries later — so the word should be read Moses, as it stands in some manuscripts and in the Vulgate, the Jews having suspended a letter above the word because they thought it a reproach to their legislator that his grandson should be an idolater. He reports Calmet's conclusion that Jonathan's line served at Dan only while the house of the Lord stood at Shiloh, until the ark was taken by the Philistines in Eli's last year, and passes on Houbigant's proposal that the text should read not the captivity of the land but the captivity of the ark, two letters being easily confounded. He ends by refusing the charge of idolatry altogether: the Danites were the first dissenters from the established worship but departed from its forms as little as they could, worshipping in the same manner though not the same place, and he believes they worshipped the true God according to their light, though the means they chose were not the best.

Ellicott presses the connection with Jeroboam, that if this image was in the shape of a calf the tradition of the cult may have made his innovation easier, and assumes the image was never dissociated from the worship of God, since Jonathan and the Danites name him Elohim, Micah for all his images calls him Jehovah, and the priest's own name means the gift of Jehovah. On the genealogy he sets out the mechanism: without the vowel points the two names differ by a single letter, and in the Masoretic text that letter is not boldly written but timidly and furtively suspended above the line, to hide the painful fact from the uninitiated; Rabbi Tanchum grants that Moses is written though Manasseh is read, and the Talmud, admitting the descent, says Scripture assigns him to Manasseh's family because he did Manasseh's deeds, a later rabbi explaining the suspended letter as making him son of Manasseh by imitation and son of Moses by blood. He will not have the sacred writer blamed for the pious fraud, which belongs to the Masoretic editors. That Jonathan was the actual grandson he thinks scarcely doubtful, since he is contemporary with Phinehas, who was beyond question Aaron's own grandson, and he finds in the speed of the fall a likely reason for the eclipse of the family of Moses. On the last verse he corrects the English, the verb being not the one rendered set up just before but meaning that the image was entrusted to Jonathan's descendants, dates the term by the sack of Shiloh, and suspects the verse was added by a later hand to prevent the earlier being misread.

sides.position: Moses; no Manasseh fits, and the reading rests on a letter the scribes suspended above the line out of reverence for the legislator
